title: A Whole Torah Verse of Measurements
subtitle: Wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, dates — one verse read as a catalog of halachic measures, then whether "measures" are really written in the Torah at all.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 1-3 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 6. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).
before: 5b ended mid-objection: the Gemara claimed "measures" (like the sukkah's 10 tefachim) are oral tradition, not Torah-derived — then immediately challenged itself, since a verse about the seven species is read as a whole catalog of measures. This amud runs through that catalog, one species at a time.

Then the same push-and-pull repeats for two more categories — interpositions that invalidate a mikveh immersion, and the minimum height of a partition — each time asking: is this really from a verse, or is the verse just a mnemonic support for something transmitted orally?

flow.label: The seven-species verse, read as seven measures
flow.sub: wheat → tzaraat-house timing · barley → a bone fragment's impurity · grapes → a nazir's wine · figs → Shabbos carrying · pomegranates → when a broken vessel stops being a vessel · olive-oil → most measures generally · dates → Yom Kippur eating

flow.label: Gemara catches its own overreach
flow.sub: "a land whose measures are olives" can't literally mean all of them — this verse lists several that aren't olive-sized. Corrected to "most."

flow.label: So are measures Torah-derived after all?
No — the verse is a mere support (asmachta); the real source is oral tradition
Same question, asked again for two more categories

items.label: Interpositions (chatzitzin)
items.sub: challenged from an explicit verse — but the oral tradition turns out to cover a narrower case (hair) than the verse does (skin)

items.label: Partitions (mechitzin)
items.sub: the 10-tefachim minimum — continues onto 6b, where it turns out to depend on whose cubit-count you follow

flowCaption: A whole verse mined for measures, then the same "verse or oral tradition" question run twice more.

opinions.claim: The entire verse "a land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and figs, and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey" is stated specifically to teach halachic measures — one per item.
opinions.basis: Deuteronomy 8:8, read as a structured list rather than a description of the land's produce.

opinions.claim: Halachic measures are not actually derived from this verse — they're halachah l'Moshe mi'Sinai (transmitted orally), and the verse is only an asmachta, a supportive mnemonic.
opinions.basis: If the measures were truly textual, they'd be spelled out per-halachah in the Torah itself — they aren't.

script.speaker: The seven species, one by one
script.gloss: Wheat — the time to eat half a loaf, for how long tzaraat-impurity is delayed when entering an afflicted house while dressed. Barley — a bone fragment that size transmits impurity by touch or carrying, but not by "tent." Grapes — a quarter-log of wine, the amount that makes a nazir liable. Figs — a dried-fig-bulk, the minimum for Shabbos carrying liability. Pomegranates — the size hole that ends a wooden vessel's ability to hold impurity. Olive oil — most measures generally. Honey (dates) — a large date-bulk, the minimum for Yom Kippur eating liability.

script.speaker: Gemara catches itself
script.quote: ״כָּל שִׁיעוּרֶיהָ״ סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ?! הָא אִיכָּא הָנֵי דְּאָמְרִינַן!
script.gloss: Wait — "a land whose measures are ALL olive-sized" can't be literal, since this very list just gave several measures that aren't olive-bulks.

script.speaker: Corrected
script.gloss: Say instead: most of its measures are olive-sized — true for the bulk of forbidden-food and impurity laws, even if this list's other items aren't.

script.speaker: Gemara challenges the whole premise
script.gloss: So measures really are Torah-derived, from this verse — not oral tradition after all!

script.speaker: Rejected
script.quote: וְתִסְבְּרָא? שִׁיעוּרִין מִי כְּתִיבִי? אֶלָּא הִלְכְתָא נִינְהוּ, וּקְרָא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא.
script.gloss: Think about it — are these measures actually spelled out per-law anywhere in the Torah? They're not. They're halachah l'Moshe mi'Sinai; the verse is only a supportive mnemonic (asmachta), not the real source.

script.speaker: Same question, category two
script.quote: חֲצִיצִין דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא נִינְהוּ! דִּכְתִיב: ״וְרָחַץ אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ בַּמַּיִם״.
script.gloss: What about interpositions that invalidate a mikveh immersion — isn't that explicitly textual? "He shall bathe his flesh in water" implies nothing may come between the flesh and the water.

script.speaker: Narrowed, not rejected
script.gloss: When the orally-transmitted halachah "arrives," it's not teaching about skin at all (that part genuinely is textual) — it's teaching about hair: per Rabbah bar bar Chana, one knotted hair interposes, three don't, and the law for two is unknown.

script.speaker: Pushed again
script.gloss: But hair is textual too — the extra word "et" in "et besaro" (his flesh) includes what's subordinate to the flesh, meaning hair!

script.speaker: Narrowed again, continuing to 6b
script.gloss: Then the oral tradition must be teaching something even narrower still — a distinction the Gemara spells out on 6b, between a majority one is particular about versus a minority one isn't.

tosfos.summary: Whether "a quarter-log of wine for a nazir" means drinking that amount, or using it to measure something else entirely — Rashi vs. Rabbeinu Tam read different texts of the underlying sugya in Nazir.

points.label: (a)-(b) Rashi's readings
points.he: פי׳ בקונטרס כדי רביעית... ובריש עירובין פי׳ בקונטרס גפן כדי רביעית יין לנזיר לחייבו מלקות
points.en: Rashi (here, and again in Eruvin) explains straightforwardly: a nazir who drinks a quarter-log of wine is liable for lashes.

points.label: (i) Rabbeinu Tam's text
points.he: ור״ת גריס שם בנזיר ת״ק לא מדמה להו לכל איסורי נזיר לאכילה
points.en: Rabbeinu Tam has a different text of the parallel sugya in Nazir, under which the amount for eating (grapes, pits, skins) is universally an olive-bulk, and only drinking wine itself is measured by a quarter-log — avoiding a difficulty about mixing eating- and drinking-measures.

tosfos.summary: Reconciling the pomegranate-sized-hole rule here with a parallel Gemara in Shabbos that uses an olive-sized hole instead.

points.label: (b) Implied Question
points.he: והא דאמר בסוף המצניע חמש מדות בכלי חרס ניקב כמוציא זית טהור מלקבל זיתים
points.en: Shabbos (95b) says a hole the size of an olive already purifies an earthenware vessel from holding olives — contradicting our pomegranate measure.

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: היינו אם יחדו לרמונים אבל סתמו כמוציא זית
points.en: That's specifically for a vessel designated for olives; a vessel with no specific designation needs the larger, pomegranate-sized hole.

tosfos.summary: What the Mishnah in Keilim means by a hole "the size of three pomegranates holding onto each other" — not three pomegranates' worth of hole, just one pomegranate of a specific middling size.

points.label: (b)-(c) Two explanations
points.he: יש לפרש דהא דנקט שלשה רמונים אחוזים... עוד יש לפרש דנקט שלשה אחוזים זה בזה משום דרמון דגדל יחידי... גדול יותר מדאי
points.en: Either: a hole big enough that three pomegranates could fall out one after another without jamming; or: "three growing together" identifies the specific middling pomegranate-size meant (solo-grown ones are oversized, four-clustered ones undersized).

tosfos.summary: Our sugya's version helps correct the text of a parallel discussion in Yoma about measures vs. punishments.

points.label: (a)-(e) Textual correction
points.he: מכאן קשה לגירסת הספרים דבפ׳ בתרא דיומא... ומתוך כך גריס התם בקונטרס עונשין מיכתב כתיבי
points.en: Some texts of Yoma (80a) have the challenge "aren't measures written?" — but our sugya already establishes the verse is a mere asmachta, so that challenge wouldn't make sense there. Rashi's version fixes it: the real challenge in Yoma is about punishments, not measures.
